page: Vultr vhp-4c-8gb-intel is a High Performance family virtual server featuring an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor with 4 shared vCPUs mapped from 2 physical cores (2 threads per core) running at 2.0 GHz. The system is equipped with 8.0 GB of RAM, yielding 2.0 GB per core, and includes 180 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. It features 16 MB of L3 cache and supports hardware-level instructions such as AVX-512 VNNI and AES cryptography.

Benchmark evaluations indicate average single-core performance, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1450.08 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1165.0. However, multi-core and memory-intensive operations show limitations, with stress-ng multi-core and Geekbench multi-core scores falling into the weak category. Memory bandwidth tests show high cached read speeds of 416.34 GB/sec, but uncached large-block reads drop to 33.43 GB/sec. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression is particularly constrained, registering in the bottom 10% of performance.

Given its shared CPU allocation and 1:2 RAM-to-vCPU ratio, this instance offers a cost-effective entry point for compute-focused workloads that do not require dedicated physical cores. The bundled 180 GB NVMe SSD provides fast local storage, but the shared CPU model and weak multi-core scaling make it less suitable for heavy database operations, complex compilation, or large-scale web serving. It is best suited for lightweight single-threaded tasks, basic text processing, Redis caching, or development environments.
description: The Vultr vhp-4c-8gb-intel is an x86_64 virtual server from the High Performance family, configured with 4 shared Intel Xeon vCPUs, 8.0 GB of RAM, and 180 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Operating at 2.0 GHz, the processor supports AVX-512 VNNI and AES instructions. Performance benchmarks reveal average single-core capabilities, such as a Geekbench single-core score of 1165.0 and strong Redis SET performance at 6.06 million operations per second. However, multi-core scaling and memory bandwidth under heavy uncached loads are weak, as evidenced by lower multi-core Geekbench and PassMark scores. This resource profile represents a budget-friendly option for workloads with moderate compute demands. It is best suited for lightweight single-threaded applications, Redis caching, basic text processing, and non-production development environments where dedicated CPU resources are not critical.
